subtopics.title: main idea and supporting evidence
subtopics.teaching: The main idea is the central point of a passage; supporting evidence includes details, examples, reasons or facts that develop that point.
subtopics.worked_example: If a passage explains how regular reading improves vocabulary and then gives several examples, the vocabulary benefit is the main idea and the examples are supporting evidence.
subtopics.pitfall: A vivid detail is not automatically the main idea.
subtopics.mastery: State the central idea and select details that directly support it.

subtopics.title: inference from explicit clues
subtopics.teaching: An inference is a reasonable conclusion supported by clues in the text rather than a sentence copied directly from it.
subtopics.worked_example: If a character carries an umbrella, wears a raincoat and avoids puddles, rain is a reasonable inference even if the passage never says 'it is raining.'
subtopics.pitfall: An inference must be supported by textual evidence, not personal imagination.
subtopics.mastery: Make inferences by combining explicit clues and rejecting unsupported assumptions.

subtopics.title: sequence cause and effect
subtopics.teaching: Sequence identifies the order of events; cause explains why something happens and effect describes what follows.
subtopics.worked_example: A storm causes a power cut, which then causes a computer to shut down: the storm is an earlier cause and the shutdown is a later effect.
subtopics.pitfall: The first event in a passage is not necessarily the cause of every later event.
subtopics.mastery: Trace chronological order and distinguish causes from consequences.

subtopics.title: author purpose and tone
subtopics.teaching: Author purpose describes why a text was written, such as to inform, explain, persuade or entertain. Tone describes the writer's attitude.
subtopics.worked_example: A notice giving exam timings mainly informs, while an advertisement encouraging readers to buy a product aims to persuade.
subtopics.pitfall: Purpose and tone are related but not identical.
subtopics.mastery: Identify purpose from content and tone from word choice and attitude.

subtopics.title: fact opinion and interpretation
subtopics.teaching: A fact can be checked against evidence; an opinion expresses a judgment or belief; an interpretation explains meaning from available evidence.
subtopics.worked_example: 'The library opens at 9 a.m.' is checkable, while 'The library is the best place in town' is an opinion.
subtopics.pitfall: An opinion can sound confident without becoming a fact.
subtopics.mastery: Classify statements and justify the classification from the wording and evidence.

subtopics.title: context clues
subtopics.teaching: Context clues are nearby words or sentences that help determine an unfamiliar word's meaning.
subtopics.worked_example: In 'The glass was fragile, so it broke when dropped,' the consequence supplies a clue that fragile means easily broken.
subtopics.pitfall: Choosing the most familiar dictionary meaning can be wrong when context points to another sense.
subtopics.mastery: Infer word meaning using surrounding evidence before selecting an option.

subtopics.title: synonyms and antonyms
subtopics.teaching: Synonyms have similar meanings and antonyms have contrasting meanings, but the relationship depends on context and part of speech.
subtopics.worked_example: 'Rapid' and 'swift' are close synonyms when describing movement; 'rapid' and 'slow' are contrasts.
subtopics.pitfall: Words that look related are not necessarily interchangeable in every sentence.
subtopics.mastery: Select a synonym or antonym that fits both meaning and grammatical use.

subtopics.title: word families
subtopics.teaching: A word family contains related forms built around a common base, often changing part of speech or grammatical function.
subtopics.worked_example: Decide, decision and decisive share a base idea but serve different grammatical roles.
subtopics.pitfall: Related words can differ in meaning enough that replacing one with another changes the sentence.
subtopics.mastery: Use word-family relationships to infer meaning and choose the correct form.

subtopics.title: roots prefixes and suffixes
subtopics.teaching: Roots carry core meaning while prefixes and suffixes modify meaning or grammatical role.
subtopics.worked_example: 'Un-' can reverse meaning in words such as unhappy; '-less' can indicate absence, as in careless.
subtopics.pitfall: A prefix or suffix does not always give a complete definition without context.
subtopics.mastery: Break unfamiliar words into meaningful parts and test the resulting meaning against context.

subtopics.title: precision in word choice
subtopics.teaching: Precise word choice selects the word that conveys the intended meaning, strength and tone most accurately.
subtopics.worked_example: 'Stroll' suggests a relaxed walk, while 'march' suggests purposeful movement; both relate to walking but are not interchangeable.
subtopics.pitfall: Using a broad synonym can remove an important distinction.
subtopics.mastery: Choose vocabulary based on meaning, context, intensity and tone.

subtopics.title: parts of speech
subtopics.teaching: Parts of speech describe grammatical roles such as noun, verb, adjective, adverb, pronoun, preposition and conjunction.
subtopics.worked_example: In 'The bright bird flew quickly,' bird is a noun, bright an adjective, flew a verb and quickly an adverb.
subtopics.pitfall: A word's part of speech can depend on how it functions in a sentence.
subtopics.mastery: Identify words by their function in the sentence, not by memorized appearance alone.

subtopics.title: sentence structure
subtopics.teaching: A complete sentence normally expresses a complete thought and contains an appropriate subject and predicate; clauses can be independent or dependent.
subtopics.worked_example: 'Because the rain stopped' is dependent and incomplete by itself, while 'The match resumed' is an independent clause.
subtopics.pitfall: Adding a capital letter and full stop does not turn a fragment into a complete sentence.
subtopics.mastery: Identify sentence boundaries and distinguish complete clauses from fragments.

subtopics.title: subject verb agreement
subtopics.teaching: The finite verb must agree with its subject in number and person.
subtopics.worked_example: 'The list of names is on the desk' uses is because list, not names, is the subject.
subtopics.pitfall: A nearby plural noun can distract from the true singular subject.
subtopics.mastery: Locate the grammatical subject before choosing the verb form.

subtopics.title: verb tenses
subtopics.teaching: Verb tense locates an action in time and can show relationships between events.
subtopics.worked_example: 'She finished the work before the teacher arrived' uses past forms to show two completed events, with before establishing their order.
subtopics.pitfall: Changing tense without a reason can make time relationships unclear.
subtopics.mastery: Choose tense from the intended time reference and relationship between actions.

subtopics.title: pronouns and modifiers
subtopics.teaching: Pronouns replace nouns; modifiers describe or limit words. Both should have clear references and logical placement.
subtopics.worked_example: In 'After reading the book, Maya wrote a review,' Maya is the person who read the book, so the modifier is logically attached.
subtopics.pitfall: A misplaced modifier can accidentally suggest that the wrong subject performed an action.
subtopics.mastery: Use clear pronoun references and place modifiers next to the words they logically describe.
